title: "Introduction"
numbered: true
bibliography: refs/thesis.bib
---

In recent decades, educational justice has emerged as a concept that has gained prominence in the study of educational inequalities. This trend has been driven by the expansion of market-based reforms in educational contexts and growing evidence of their harmful effects on equity [@francis_social_2017; @camphuijsen_publicprivate_2026; @sciffer_does_2022]. In the Chilean context, the commodification of education has led to the adoption of a “consumer-provider” logic, in which the educational system ends up mimicking market dynamics [@corvalan_mercado_2016]. These processes have consolidated an educational market that does not ensure equal access to opportunities, as financial barriers act as a prerequisite for enrollment in certain schools. Beyond that, the main problem is that, within this logic of competition, private schools offer a higher quality of education than public schools, a fact consistently demonstrated by national standardized tests [@bellei_problema_2025]. These reforms do not merely entail changes in institutional architecture; they also implicitly alter the way people understand education. Thus, in a scenario where education operates under market forces, the concept of “market justice” becomes highly relevant for a deeper understanding of this process. As proposed by @lane_market_1986, “market justice” refers to the normative beliefs that legitimize the idea that access to and the quality of services—such as education—depend on the ability to pay [@lindh_public_2015]. Educational justice (as well as social justice) is at odds with market justice, since while the former seeks to level the playing field regarding background inequalities and guarantee equal opportunities regardless of social status, market justice defends educational inequality from the outset by limiting opportunities based on families’ purchasing power [@moyano_justicia_2020; @walzer_spheres_2010; @deutsch_equity_1975].

The justification for inequalities in education can be understood through classic self-interest hypotheses, in which people with higher status defend their social position by supporting the market or opposing redistribution. However, there are other factors that are equally important, if not more so, in this area, such as meritocracy. Known as a distributive system based on effort and talent [@young_rise_2017], meritocratic discourse attributes responsibility for success or failure to the individual. In the educational context, meritocracy lies at the heart of every educational institution, where it is presented as an ideal, promising that those who work the hardest will receive rewards commensurate with their efforts [@darnon_belief_2018]. However, outcomes are influenced by students’ family backgrounds and, more broadly, by the structural conditions of society. The meritocratic narrative overlooks the role of underlying conditions in people’s educational trajectories, thereby functioning as a mechanism for legitimizing inequality, since individuals are held responsible for their outcomes—whether success or failure [@mijs_unfulfillable_2016; @clycq_meritocracy_2014]. 

Until now, the literature has studied meritocracy with a particular focus on perceptions of effort and talent, but I argue that examining the relationship between market justice in education and meritocracy requires a broader model than one based solely on perceptions of merit. In this regard, @castillo_multidimensional_2023 proposed a conceptual framework that makes two distinctions: First, it distinguishes between perceptions and preferences. Perceptions refer to how people observe meritocracy operating in society, while preferences refer to how society should operate. Second, it distinguishes between meritocratic beliefs—which are related to effort and talent—and privilege beliefs, which are expressed through family background and social connections. Thus, the framework encompasses both perceptions and preferences regarding beliefs about meritocracy and privilege. Based on this multidimensional framework of meritocracy, evidence supports the view that meritocratic beliefs and privilege beliefs are neither opposites nor part of the same continuum, but rather distinct dimensions and can therefore coexist in people’s minds [@castillo_multidimensional_2023].

Previous studies have examined the relationship between market justice and meritocracy finding positive asociations, but without a multidimensional framework to observe how meritocratic beliefs operate alongside those based on privilege [@castillo_socialization_2024; @castillo_perceptions_2025; @castillo_justification_2026]. Similarly, most studies examining market justice and meritocracy have relied on variable-centered methods, which make it impossible to determine whether beliefs are heterogeneous within the population [@castillo_perceptions_2025; @castillo_justification_2026]. This research aims to contribute to the agenda of meritocracy and market justice in two ways: First, I apply a novel person-centered approach, which assumes not everyone shares the same beliefs, allowing us to identify patterns of belief based on shared attributes—an approach that is uncommon in sociological studies [@vanhootegem_worlds_2022; @zhu_meritocratic_2025]. This makes possible to observe how meritocratic and privilege-related beliefs are organized in people’s minds in terms of the number and size of groups. Furthermore, I am seeking to understand how each group relates to market justice in education, hoping to discover new perspectives by studying the diversity of beliefs about merit alongside privilege. The latest contribution aims to demonstrate that there is a complex interplay between meritocracy and the legitimacy of inequalities that is not straightforward. 

Based on the literature, the main argument is that where merit-based beliefs predominate, their relationship with market justice in education will be positive, reinforcing the narrative of meritocracy as a legitimizer of inequalities. Thus, the two research questions underlying this study are: (1) How do meritocratic and privilege belief patterns manifest themselves in terms of the number of identifiable groups and their size? (2) How do different groups of people, based on meritocratic and privilege-based beliefs, relate to market justice in education?

This study is particularly relevant in Chile, a country characterized by high levels of inequality and a system in which social goods are highly commodified [@boccardo_30_2020; @castillo_changes_2025]. The neoliberal reforms of the civil-military dictatorship (1973–1989) have produced structurally segmented systems in health care, pensions, and education, in which access and quality depend on ability to pay, benefiting higher-income sectors and relegating the poorest to limited, underfunded public alternatives [@madariaga_three_2020]. Specifically, the education system is highlighted as one of the most privatized in the world, where the quality of private education surpasses that of public education due to limited regulation of the education market, as reflected in high levels of school segregation and low regard for public education [@bellei_problema_2025; @bellei_gran_2016; @ramos_educacion_2022; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2014]. To address these issues, a series of policies have been developed in recent years with the goal of reducing school segregation and lowering barriers in access to education [@bellei_models_2023]. Despite this, people continue to hold strong meritocratic beliefs, illustrating the inequality paradox [@pnud_desiguales_2017; @mijs_paradox_2021]. Thus, in a context marked by high and durable inequalities, deep marketization of education, and the entrenchment of meritocratic beliefs, it is relevant to examine the link between meritocratic beliefs and market-justice preferences in education.
